items.stem: A daemon needs to shut down and should be given the chance to flush buffers, close files, and release its lock before it stops. Which signal, and which command, is the right first move?

options.text: SIGTERM, sent with plain `kill <pid>`, since it asks the process to shut down and can be caught
options.why: `kill` sends SIGTERM by default, and unlike SIGKILL it can be caught by a handler that performs an orderly shutdown.

options.text: SIGKILL, sent with `kill -9 <pid>`, to guarantee the process actually stops
options.why: SIGKILL removes the process from the scheduler immediately with no chance to clean up, which is the opposite of what an orderly shutdown needs as a first move.

options.text: SIGSTOP, to pause the process before deciding what to do next — a process flushes its buffers to disk as part of entering the stopped state
options.why: SIGSTOP freezes the process rather than asking it to exit, and it cannot be caught or handled by the program at all.

options.text: SIGHUP, since it is the standard signal for terminating a daemon cleanly
options.why: SIGHUP is conventionally used to ask a daemon to reload its configuration, not to terminate it.

items.stem: `kill -9` is sent to a process stuck reading from an unresponsive network filesystem, and the process is still there afterward. What explains this apparent failure?

options.text: The process is in uninterruptible sleep, waiting inside the kernel on I/O, and cannot be reaped until that I/O returns or times out
options.why: A process blocked in the kernel on I/O is not in a position to respond to any signal, including SIGKILL, until the kernel call it is stuck in resolves.

options.why: Ownership would produce a permission error immediately, not a process that appears to survive the signal indefinitely.

items.stem: An unprivileged user wants to lower the nice value of their own running batch job from 10 to 0, to give it more CPU time. Can they do it with plain `renice`?

options.text: No — lowering a nice value requires root or `CAP_SYS_NICE`, unless the administrator has raised `RLIMIT_NICE`, which by default allows no reduction

items.stem: A batch job is niced all the way down to 19 but a database it is supposedly starving is still slow. `top` shows the machine is not CPU-bound; memory usage is very high and swap activity is heavy. Will renicing the batch job further help?

options.text: No — nice only biases CPU scheduling, and it does nothing for memory pressure or I/O waits

options.why: `apt upgrade` already installs newer versions; `full-upgrade` is a variant that is additionally permitted to remove packages to complete the upgrade.

items.stem: A team runs `apt upgrade -y` on every server the moment any update becomes available, with no staging tier and no rollback plan. Are they practicing patch management?

options.text: No — patch management is the surrounding discipline (inventory, testing, scheduled rollout, rollback), not merely running an update command
options.why: Running the command is only the final step of the practice; without testing, scheduling and a rollback path, untested changes reach production directly.

options.text: Yes, applying updates the moment they appear is the definition of good patch management
options.why: Applying every update immediately, untested, on production is a change-management failure rather than diligence — it is how a patch causes the outage it was meant to prevent.

options.text: No, because patch management applies only to security updates, not general package upgrades
options.why: The practice applies to updates generally, though security updates are often prioritised and sometimes automated separately for exactly that reason.

options.text: Yes, provided the updates are also logged somewhere after they are applied — that record is what turns ad-hoc updating into managed patching
options.why: Logging what happened after the fact does not substitute for the testing, staged rollout and rollback plan the practice requires beforehand; NIST's definition centres on identifying, prioritising, acquiring, installing and verifying patches, not on recording them afterwards.

items.rationale: Patch management is the disciplined practice around updates — inventory, tracking advisories, testing before production, applying on a schedule, and being able to roll back — not simply the act of running an update command. Applying every update immediately and untested is a change-management failure, not the practice itself.

items.stem: Someone asks "what filesystem does the FHS use?" What is wrong with the question?

options.text: The FHS is not a filesystem at all; it is a convention for what each directory means, not an on-disk format
options.why: The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard names directory purposes such as `/etc` and `/var`; journaling and on-disk layout belong to a completely separate concept, the filesystem type.

options.why: The FHS says nothing about journaling, block size, or maximum file size — those are properties of a filesystem type, a distinct concept that happens to share the word "filesystem" — and it defines no on-disk format at all, default or otherwise.

options.text: The question is fine, and the answer is whichever filesystem type the root partition uses
options.why: The FHS applies identically regardless of which on-disk format is chosen underneath it; the two are independent concepts sharing a name.

options.text: The question is fine, and the answer is `tmpfs`, since that is what most FHS directories use
options.why: Most FHS-defined directories sit on whatever the administrator chose at `mkfs` time, not universally on `tmpfs`.

items.rationale: The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard is a naming convention — what `/etc`, `/var`, `/usr` and the rest are for — not an on-disk format. Filesystem type (ext4, XFS, Btrfs, and so on) is the entirely separate concept that determines journaling, block size and maximum file size.

items.stem: A team is choosing where to install software they compiled themselves, separate from anything the distribution's package manager owns. Which directory is the standard place, and why not `/usr/bin`?

options.text: `/usr/local`, because the package manager owns everything under `/usr` except that subtree
options.why: The `/usr/local` tree exists precisely so locally built software cannot be overwritten by a package update to the rest of `/usr`.

options.text: `/usr/bin`, since that is simply where all executables belong regardless of who built them
options.why: The package manager treats everything under `/usr/bin` as its own; placing locally compiled software there risks it being overwritten by the next package update.

options.text: `/opt`, since any third-party software belongs there by convention
options.why: `/opt` is for self-contained third-party packages that keep their own directory tree, a different pattern from software built to install into the normal hierarchy.

options.text: `/var/local`, since locally built software is variable data
options.why: Locally compiled software is static once installed, not data that grows at runtime, so it does not belong under `/var`.

items.rationale: The FHS reserves `/usr/local` as the parallel tree for software the local administrator builds and installs, kept separate from everything the package manager owns under `/usr`. `/opt` is the related but distinct convention for self-contained third-party packages with their own tree.

items.stem: Which directory holds host-specific system configuration, and what does the FHS say may never be placed there?

options.text: `/etc`, and binaries — the FHS is explicit that `/etc` holds settings, not the programs that read them
options.why: The classification "unshareable and static" is what makes `/etc` the natural place for configuration text files rather than executables.

options.why: Log files belong under `/var/log`, since they are variable data that grows at runtime — a different classification from `/etc`'s static configuration.

options.text: `/var`, and binaries, since `/var` is also host-specific
options.why: `/var` is unshareable and variable, holding logs and runtime state, not the static configuration that `/etc` holds.

options.text: `/usr/local/etc`, and configuration files themselves — since FHS 3.0 moved system-wide configuration out of `/etc` and into that tree
options.why: FHS 3.0 still defines `/etc` as host-specific system configuration and it is exactly configuration files that belong there; `/usr/local/etc` is defined only as host-specific configuration for locally installed binaries, not as a replacement for `/etc`.

items.stem: A service on the host stops writing its logs and refuses to start, while every other service on the machine keeps working normally. What is the first thing to check?

options.text: Whether `/var` (or the log directory under it) has filled up, since a full `/var` is one of the most common causes of exactly this symptom
options.why: Services that cannot write logs or state files stop or refuse to start while the rest of the system keeps working, because `/var` is often its own filesystem.

options.text: Whether `/usr` has filled up, since that is where the service's program files live
options.why: `/usr` is read-only and static under normal operation; it is `/var`, holding variable data such as logs, that characteristically fills and causes this symptom.

options.why: A service typically has no meaningful presence under `/home`; the FHS places spool directories, logging data and application state under `/var`, which is where a daemon's growing files actually live.

items.stem: Where is the superuser's home directory, and why does the FHS keep it separate from `/home`?

options.text: `/root`, kept outside `/home` so the system does not need a fallback default if `/home` — often a separate partition — fails to mount

options.why: Root has its own dedicated home directory, `/root`, distinct from the filesystem root `/`.

items.stem: Why does software compiled from source conventionally install into `/usr/local/bin` rather than `/usr/bin`?

options.text: Because the package manager owns everything under `/usr` except `/usr/local`, and installing there avoids being silently overwritten
options.why: Keeping locally built software in its own subtree is what protects it from being clobbered when the package manager updates the rest of `/usr`.

options.text: Because `/usr/local/bin` is searched earlier in `$PATH` on every distribution by default
options.why: `$PATH` ordering is a separate configuration choice and is not the reason the FHS reserves this subtree for locally built software.

options.text: Because `/usr/bin` is reserved exclusively for binaries shipped with the kernel itself — the FHS lists it among the directories that must hold nothing outside the base kernel image
options.why: FHS 4.4 titles `/usr/bin` "Most user commands"; it holds ordinary user-land programs installed by the distribution's package manager and is not tied to the kernel.

items.stem: What does the FHS say a program may assume about the contents of `/tmp` between two separate invocations?

options.text: Nothing, because programs must not assume anything left there is preserved between invocations
options.why: The FHS is explicit on this point, and on many systems `/tmp` is cleared on reboot or actively aged out, reinforcing that nothing there should be relied upon to persist.

items.stem: An administrator writes a new value to `/proc/sys/vm/swappiness` to change kernel tuning immediately. Does that change survive the next reboot?

options.text: No — the change applies to the running kernel immediately but is lost at the next boot unless also recorded under `/etc/sysctl.d/`
options.why: Writes under `/proc/sys` take effect on the live kernel right away, but persistence across a reboot needs the same setting recorded in configuration read at startup.

options.text: Yes, any write under `/proc/sys` is automatically persisted to disk — the kernel mirrors each accepted write into `/etc/sysctl.conf` as it happens
options.why: `/proc` is a pseudo-filesystem generated by the kernel and writes nothing back to disk; persistence works the other way round, with `systemd-sysctl.service` reading `/etc/sysctl.d/*.conf` at boot and writing each key into `/proc/sys`.

options.why: The opposite is true: the write to `/proc/sys` takes effect on the running kernel immediately, without any reboot.

options.why: Device nodes live under `/dev` and represent hardware; `/proc/sys` is a distinct virtual filesystem exposing tunable kernel parameters as files.

items.stem: `ls -l /proc/1234/status` reports a file size of zero bytes, yet `cat`-ing it returns pages of readable text. Is that a sign of filesystem corruption?

options.text: No. Entries under `/proc` are generated by the kernel on demand, so they legitimately report zero size while still returning content when read
options.why: Reading a path under `/proc` causes the kernel to generate the contents at that moment, which is why the reported size and the actual read content do not match the way an ordinary file would.

options.text: No, but it does mean the process's inode has been exhausted — `/proc` allocates one inode per open file descriptor and drops the reported size to zero once that pool runs out
options.why: Inode exhaustion is a property of on-disk filesystems with a fixed inode table; `/proc` entries are generated by the kernel on read and consume no on-disk inodes, and the zero size is unconditional rather than a symptom of anything.

options.text: Yes, and the fix is to remount the filesystem `/proc` lives on
options.why: Nothing about this symptom indicates a mount problem; it is the expected, permanent behaviour of every entry under `/proc`.

items.stem: What is the behavioural difference between reading from `/dev/null` and reading from `/dev/zero`?

options.why: The two pseudo-devices differ specifically in what a read from them produces: nothing at all versus an unbounded stream of zero bytes.

options.why: They agree on write behaviour (both discard input), but they behave very differently on read, which the "general-purpose discard" framing misses.

options.text: `/dev/null` is a block device and `/dev/zero` is a character device

items.stem: A team plans to grow a filesystem while it stays mounted, and possibly shrink it later. Between ext4 and XFS, which choice keeps the shrink option open?

items.stem: A backup script tries `ln /data/report.csv /backup/report.csv` across two different mounted filesystems, and it fails. Switching to `ln -s` succeeds. Why the difference?

options.text: A hard link refers to an inode number, meaningful only within one filesystem, so it cannot cross a filesystem boundary; a symlink stores a path and has no such restriction
options.why: Because a hard link is a directory entry bound to an inode number, and inode numbers are only meaningful within one filesystem, link(2) fails with EXDEV when the two paths are not on the same mounted filesystem; `ln -s` merely stores a path string, which carries no such restriction.

options.text: `ln` is simply broken for this use case and `ln -s` should always be preferred instead
options.why: `ln` works correctly within a single filesystem; the failure here is specifically the cross-filesystem restriction, not a general defect.

options.text: The destination directory must not have existed yet, which only `ln -s` tolerates
options.why: Nothing in the scenario indicates a missing destination directory; the described failure is the standard cross-filesystem restriction on hard links.

options.text: `/backup` must be a read-only mount, which blocks `ln` but not `ln -s` — a symbolic link is recorded in the source directory rather than the destination, so a read-only target never comes into it
options.why: Both link types create a new entry in the destination directory, so a read-only `/backup` would fail for `ln -s` just as readily; the failure described is link(2)'s EXDEV, raised when the two paths are not on the same mounted filesystem.

items.rationale: A hard link is a reference to an inode number, and inode numbers are meaningful only within one filesystem, so `ln` refuses to create one across a filesystem boundary. A symbolic link stores a path string instead and has no such restriction, which is why `ln -s` succeeds where `ln` does not.

verification.reasoning: CITATION FIX: the concept cited `man-inode-7` alone, which never states the cross-filesystem restriction. Added link(2), ln(1) and symlink(7). Key confirmed against link(2)'s ERRORS section: "EXDEV — oldpath and newpath are not on the same mounted filesystem." symlink(7) supplies the contrast: a symbolic link is "a special type of file whose contents are a string that is the pathname of another file", so it carries no inode reference and no filesystem constraint. o2 `why` true — ln(1) creates hard links correctly within one filesystem, so the failure is the specific EXDEV restriction rather than a defect. o3 `why` true: nothing in the stem indicates a missing destination directory, and a missing directory would fail for `ln -s` as well. o4 was SELF-REFUTING as authored (text carried its own `why` after an em-dash); rewritten with a real false mechanism, refuted by the fact that both link types write an entry into the destination directory. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: `df -h` reports a filesystem at 100% used, but `du -sh` walking the same filesystem from the top totals far less than what `df` reports. What kind of cause does that gap point at?

options.text: A structural cause invisible to `du` — most commonly a deleted file still held open by a running process
options.why: A deleted-but-open file keeps its blocks allocated on the filesystem, but has no name left for `du` to walk to, so it never appears in the total.

options.text: `du` must simply be miscounting, and rerunning it with different flags will resolve the discrepancy
options.why: `du` is not miscounting; it fundamentally cannot see certain categories of space, such as a deleted-but-open file, regardless of which flags are used.

options.text: The filesystem must have run out of inodes rather than blocks — an exhausted inode table is billed to `df` as used space while contributing nothing that `du` can walk to
options.why: Inode exhaustion shows up in `df -i`, not as inflated block usage in `df -h`; it produces "No space left on device" on new writes while blocks remain free, and does not open a gap between reported used space and a directory walk.

options.text: The discrepancy always means the filesystem needs an `fsck` before anything else is checked
options.why: A structural check is not the standard first response to this specific symptom; `df` and `du` disagreeing has well-known, non-corruption causes to check first.

items.rationale: `df` reports what the filesystem itself has allocated, which includes blocks belonging to files that have been unlinked but are still held open by a running process; `du` walks directory names and cannot see such a file at all, since it has no name left to walk to. That is the classic explanation when `du`'s total falls well short of `df`'s.

verification.reasoning: CITATION FIX, and the exact miss this pass exists to catch: the concept cited `man-mount-8` and `man-inode-7` for a claim about deleted-but-open files. Neither documents it — that behaviour is unlink(2). Re-cited to unlink(2), du(1) and df(1). unlink(2) settles the key: "If the name was the last link to a file but any processes still have the file open, the file will remain in existence until the last file descriptor referring to it is closed" — blocks still allocated, no name left. du(1) supplies the other half of the gap: "Summarize device usage of the set of FILEs, recursively for directories," i.e. it can only total what it can reach by walking names, so a nameless-but-open file is structurally invisible to it, whereas df(1) reports the filesystem's own accounting. o2 `why` true and follows directly: no du flag can reach a file with no remaining name. o3 was SELF-REFUTING as authored (text carried its own `why` after an em-dash); rewritten with a real false mechanism, and the corrected `why` is checked against df(1) "-i, --inodes — list inode information instead of block usage". o4 `why` true. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A filesystem reports full. Walk through the correct diagnostic order: what is checked first, second, and third?

options.text: `df -h` to find which filesystem is full, then `df -i` to rule out inode exhaustion, then `du -sh` descending from the mount point to locate the largest tree
options.why: Working outward from the cheapest check identifies which filesystem, then which resource (blocks or inodes), then which directory is actually responsible.

options.text: `du -sh /` immediately, since it directly finds the largest files on the whole machine in one pass
options.why: Running `du` over the entire machine first skips identifying which filesystem is actually affected and wastes time walking filesystems that are not the problem.

options.text: `lsof +L1` first, since deleted-but-open files are always the cause of a full filesystem — every other cause of a full filesystem will already have been reported as an error long before `df` shows 100%
options.why: Deleted-but-open files are one possible cause among several, and nothing reports the ordinary ones in advance; checking for them before confirming which filesystem and which resource is full is out of order.

options.text: `fsck` immediately, since a full filesystem should always be checked for structural damage first
options.why: A full filesystem is not itself evidence of corruption, and running `fsck` first skips the cheap checks that usually explain the symptom directly.

items.rationale: The efficient order works outward from the cheapest check: `df -h` identifies which filesystem is full, `df -i` on that filesystem rules in or out inode exhaustion, and only then does `du -sh` descending from the mount point locate the specific directory responsible — checking the three structural causes (unlinked-open file, hidden mount, reserved blocks) if `du`'s total still falls short.

verification.reasoning: CITATION FIX: re-cited from `man-mount-8`/`man-inode-7` to df(1), du(1) and unlink(2), which are the pages that document each step of the key's order. Key confirmed piecewise: df(1) with no argument shows "the space available on all currently mounted file systems", which is the step that identifies which filesystem; df(1) "-i, --inodes — list inode information instead of block usage" is the step that separates blocks from inodes; du(1) "Summarize device usage of the set of FILEs, recursively for directories" is the step that localises the largest tree. The ordering claim is the pedagogical content and each step is individually sourced. o2 `why` true — running du from / walks filesystems that df would have excluded in one cheap call. o3 was SELF-REFUTING as authored: its option text carried its own `why` verbatim after an em-dash, announcing its own wrongness. Rewritten with a real false clause (a claim that every other cause is reported in advance), and the corrected `why` rests on unlink(2), which establishes that a deleted-but-open file is one possible cause of allocated-but-unwalkable space rather than the only cause of a full filesystem. o4 `why` true — a full filesystem is not evidence of structural damage. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: `free -h` shows several gigabytes of swap in use on a server that otherwise seems healthy. Is that, by itself, evidence of a memory problem?

options.text: No — swap in use and swapping in progress are different things; pages evicted hours ago and never touched since remain "used" without indicating current trouble
options.why: A non-zero swap-used figure only shows that some memory was paged out at some point; the actual warning sign is a sustained non-zero `si`/`so` in `vmstat`, which are per-second rates of paging in and out rather than a standing level.

options.text: Yes, any non-zero swap usage means the machine needs more RAM immediately
options.why: Some swap usage is normal — the kernel pages out genuinely idle memory to free RAM for cache — and does not by itself indicate a shortage.

options.text: No, but only because `free -h` cannot report swap usage accurately — it reads a cached total that is refreshed only when a swap device is added or removed, so the figure it prints can be arbitrarily stale on a long-running server
options.why: free(1) reports swap from SwapTotal and SwapFree in `/proc/meminfo`, which the kernel keeps current on every read; the difficulty is interpreting a non-zero figure, not the accuracy of the tool.

options.text: Yes, and disabling swap entirely is the correct fix for a machine under any memory pressure
options.why: Disabling swap does not remove memory pressure; it converts a slow, swapping system into one where the kernel's out-of-memory killer terminates a process instead.

items.rationale: Swap usage is a diagnostic signal that is easy to misread. Some swap in use is normal, since the kernel evicts genuinely idle pages to free RAM for cache; what actually indicates trouble is a high rate of swap-in and swap-out happening now, which `free`'s repeated sampling (`-s`) shows better than a single snapshot.

verification.reasoning: CITATION FIX: the concept cited `man-fstab-5` and `man-proc-5`, neither of which supports a claim about interpreting swap usage. Re-cited to free(1), vmstat(8) and swapon(8). The level-versus-rate distinction that the key rests on is settled by putting the two pages side by side: free(1) reports "total ... (MemTotal and SwapTotal in /proc/meminfo)" and "free — Unused memory (MemFree and SwapFree in /proc/meminfo)" — standing quantities — while vmstat(8) defines "si: Amount of memory swapped in from disk (/s)" and "so: Amount of memory swapped to disk (/s)" — per-second rates. A non-zero standing level therefore does not imply any current paging activity, which is exactly the key. o2 `why` true and consistent with those definitions. o3 was SELF-REFUTING as authored (text carried its own `why` after an em-dash); rewritten with a real false mechanism, refuted by free(1) naming /proc/meminfo as its live source. o4 `why` — that removing swap converts memory pressure into OOM-killer terminations rather than eliminating it — is supported by proc_pid_oom_score(5), which documents the kernel's out-of-memory victim selection; `man-proc-pid-oom-score` added to source_ids to cover it. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A newly created swap partition has been prepared but `swapon --show` lists nothing active, and `swapon /dev/sdb2` reports an error. What step was most likely skipped?

options.text: `mkswap` was never run on the device, so it has no swap signature for `swapon` to activate
options.why: `swapon` activates an area that has already been prepared as swap; without that preparation step there is nothing valid for it to turn on.

options.text: The partition needs to be formatted with `mkfs -t ext4` before it can be used as swap
options.why: Swap space is not a regular filesystem and is not created with `mkfs`; it is prepared specifically with `mkswap`.

options.text: An `/etc/fstab` entry must exist before `swapon` will activate any device at all
options.why: A device can be activated directly with `swapon <device>` without any fstab entry; the entry is only needed for it to activate automatically at boot.

options.text: The partition must first be added to a volume group before it can hold swap — `mkswap` refuses to write its signature to anything that is not a logical volume
options.why: mkswap(8) documents its device argument as "usually a disk partition (something like /dev/sdb7) but can also be a file"; no volume group is involved at any point.

items.rationale: Swap space is created with `mkswap`, which writes the signature `swapon` looks for, and only then activated with `swapon`. Running `swapon` on a partition that was never prepared with `mkswap` fails because there is no swap signature there for it to recognise.

verification.reasoning: CITATION FIX: the concept cited `man-fstab-5`, which covers the fstab swap entry but not the preparation step the question turns on. Re-cited to mkswap(8) and swapon(8). Key confirmed against mkswap(8): "mkswap sets up a Linux swap area on a device or in a file ... After creating the swap area, you need the swapon(8) command to start using it." An unprepared device has no swap area for swapon to activate. o2 `why` true — mkswap(8) is the tool for swap areas and swap is not a regular filesystem made with mkfs. o3 `why` confirmed by mkswap(8) — "Usually swap areas are listed in /etc/fstab so that they can be taken into use at boot time by a swapon -a command" — the fstab entry serves boot-time activation, while swapon(8) accepts a device directly. o4 was SELF-REFUTING as authored (text carried its own `why` after an em-dash); rewritten with a real false mechanism, refuted by mkswap(8)'s own description of its device argument. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: What advantage does an LVM logical volume have over a plain disk partition, which is the reason it is worth recognising for this exam?

options.text: It can be resized and can span more than one physical disk, which a plain partition cannot do
options.why: Pooling physical volumes into a volume group and carving logical volumes out of that pool is exactly what lets a volume grow, shrink or move across devices.

options.text: It is faster than a plain partition for every kind of workload — the device-mapper layer coalesces I/O so that every access path is shorter than on a raw partition
options.why: LVM adds a device-mapper abstraction for flexibility; lvm(8) presents it as providing capabilities beyond the physical devices, not as making storage faster, and speed is not the property being tested here.

options.text: It automatically protects data against drive failure, the way RAID does
options.why: Redundancy against drive failure is what RAID provides; LVM by itself is about flexible sizing and pooling, not fault tolerance.

options.text: It removes the need for a filesystem to be created on top of it
options.why: A logical volume still needs a filesystem created on it with `mkfs`, exactly like a plain partition would.

items.rationale: LVM pools physical volumes into a volume group, from which logical volumes are carved out. Its one selling point over a bare partition is that a logical volume can later be grown, shrunk, or moved across several physical disks — recognition of that three-layer vocabulary (PV, VG, LV) is the LFCA-level expectation, summarised respectively by `pvs`, `vgs` and `lvs`.

verification.reasoning: CITATION FIX: the concept cited `man-mount-8`, which never mentions LVM. Re-cited to lvm(8) and lvcreate(8). Key confirmed against lvm(8): "A Volume Group (VG) is a collection of one or more physical devices, each called a Physical Volume (PV). A Logical Volume (LV) is a virtual block device ... Each block of data in an LV is stored on one or more PV in the VG" — that is the spanning half — while the same page lists lvextend, lvreduce, lvresize and pvmove among its commands, which is the resizing half. Neither is possible with a plain partition, whose extent is fixed by the partition table on one disk. o2 was SELF-REFUTING as authored (text carried its own `why` after an em-dash, and misrendered "LVM" as "lVM"); rewritten with a real false mechanism. o3 `why` true — lvm(8) describes pooling and virtual block devices, not redundancy; RAID is a separate mechanism. o4 `why` true: an LV is a block device and still needs a filesystem created on it. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A system needs to survive the loss of any one drive while maximising usable capacity from four drives. Which RAID level fits, and how many drives does it need at minimum?

options.text: RAID 5, needing at least three drives and giving the capacity of all but one
options.why: RAID 5 stripes with distributed parity, surviving exactly one drive failure while sacrificing only one drive's worth of capacity to redundancy.

options.text: RAID 0, since striping across four drives gives the largest usable capacity of any option
options.why: RAID 0 has no redundancy at all and loses everything if any single drive fails — it does not survive a drive loss, which the requirement specifically asks for.

options.text: RAID 1, since mirroring is the simplest way to survive a drive failure
options.why: RAID 1 survives a drive loss but gives only the capacity of one drive regardless of how many are mirrored, which does not maximise usable capacity from four drives.

options.text: RAID 10, since striping across mirrored pairs also survives the loss of any one drive
options.why: RAID 10 does survive a single drive loss, but holding two copies of every block leaves only half the raw capacity usable, which is less than RAID 5's all-but-one on the same four drives.

items.rationale: RAID 5 needs at least three drives, gives the capacity of all but one, and survives exactly one drive failure — the best capacity-to-redundancy trade-off of the options for surviving a single drive loss. RAID 6, RAID 10 and RAID 1 all trade away more capacity for additional protection.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed: Red Hat's RHEL 9 RAID documentation states that a RAID level 5 array requires at least 3 disks and that 'the storage capacity of RAID level 5 is calculated the same way as with level 4' (all but one member), and md(4) states that RAID5 distributes parity across all devices so the array continues to function if one device fails. o2 (RAID 0) is wrong and its why is true — md(4) lists RAID0 among the 'pseudo RAID (non-redundant) configurations'. o3 (RAID 1) is wrong and its why is true — Red Hat states RAID 1 capacity equals the smallest mirrored member. REFUTED AS AUTHORED on o4: the distractor's why asserted 'RAID 10 needs at least four drives, correctly', which is false on Linux — the same Red Hat page describes a 3-drive level 10 array storing two copies and giving 1.5x the smallest device, and the RHEL installer text says level 10 'requires a minimum of three separate disks'. o4's text and why were rewritten to turn purely on capacity, which is the discriminator the stem asks about, and re-checked against both sources: confirmed. Citation was also refuted as authored: the concept cited proc(5), which contains nothing about RAID; fixed at concept level in data/topics/02-system-administration.json to md(4) plus the Red Hat RAID-levels chapter. Empirical verification was attempted and could NOT be run: 'docker run --rm --privileged ubuntu:24.04' with mdadm over loopback devices fails on this host because the Docker Desktop linuxkit kernel 6.12.76 ships no md_mod ('modprobe: FATAL: Module md_mod not found'), so the minimum-device claim rests on the Red Hat documentation rather than on measurement.

items.stem: A team relies on a mirrored RAID 1 array and treats it as their backup strategy. An operator accidentally deletes a critical directory. What does the mirror do?

options.text: It faithfully mirrors the deletion to the second drive just as quickly as any other write, so RAID alone does not recover the directory
options.why: RAID protects against a drive failing; it applies every write, including a deletion, to both members with equal fidelity, which is exactly why it is not a substitute for a backup.

options.text: It protects the directory, since RAID 1 keeps an independent second copy — mirrors resynchronise on a schedule rather than on every write, so the deletion has not reached the second drive yet
options.why: The second drive is kept in lockstep with the first rather than independent of it, so the "protection" a backup provides against deletion is not what mirroring gives.

options.text: It automatically preserves a prior version of the directory before the deletion, since mirrors are point-in-time
options.why: A mirror is continuously kept current with the primary, not captured at a point in time, so there is no earlier version retained anywhere in the array.

options.text: It depends on which RAID controller is used, since some controllers block destructive commands
options.why: RAID operates below the filesystem, mirroring whatever writes the operating system issues; it has no awareness of whether a given write is destructive.

items.rationale: RAID protects only against a drive failing — not against accidental deletion, corruption, or any other destructive write, all of which are mirrored or parity-protected just as faithfully as a legitimate write. That is why RAID levels are never a substitute for backups.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed by mechanism from the primary source: md(4) states that in a RAID1 array 'each device contains exactly the same data' and 'changes are written to all devices in parallel', so an unlink is applied to both members immediately and no earlier version survives; Red Hat's RAID chapter likewise describes mirroring as writing identical data to each member disk. Neither source contains the slogan 'RAID is not a backup' — recorded here as a derivation from the documented write behaviour, not as a quotation. o3's why is true (a mirror is continuously current, not point-in-time). o4's why is true (md is a block-layer driver and mirrors whatever writes it is given). REFUTED AS AUTHORED on o2: the option text carried its own refutation appended verbatim from its why ('the second drive is kept in lockstep with the first rather than independent of it...'), announcing its own wrongness. The text was rewritten to state a plausible but false mechanism (scheduled resynchronisation), which md(4) contradicts directly with 'changes are written to all devices in parallel'; the why is unchanged and remains true. Re-checked: confirmed. Citation refuted as authored and fixed at concept level (proc(5) -> md(4) + Red Hat RAID levels).

items.stem: A user wants to edit their personal crontab. Why is `crontab -e` preferred over opening the spool file under `/var/spool/cron/` directly in a text editor?

options.text: `crontab -e` validates the syntax before installing the result and ensures the daemon notices the change
options.why: Editing the spool file directly can leave the daemon unaware of the edit and bypasses the syntax check the command performs before installing anything.

options.text: There is no real difference; both approaches update the same file identically
options.why: The command path adds a validation step and guarantees the daemon picks up the change, neither of which a direct file edit provides.

options.text: Editing the spool file is preferred, since `crontab -e` only works for system crontabs, not personal ones
options.why: `crontab -e` is specifically the personal crontab editor; system crontabs under `/etc/cron.d/` are a different, separate mechanism.

options.text: `crontab -e` is required because personal crontabs cannot contain more than one line
options.why: A personal crontab can hold any number of lines; the reason to prefer the command is validation and daemon notification, not a line-count restriction.

items.rationale: A user crontab is edited through `crontab -e` because the command validates the syntax and installs the result into the spool directory the daemon watches. Editing the spool file directly can leave cron unaware of the change and skips the validation step entirely.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed on documentation and by measurement. crontab(1) states that user crontabs 'are files in /var/spool/, they are not intended to be edited directly', that -e installs the modified crontab automatically after the editor exits, and that -T tests syntax without installing. The validation claim was then verified empirically: 'docker run --rm debian:12' with cron installed, then 'crontab /tmp/bad' where /tmp/bad contained the line 'bogus line here', printed '"/tmp/bad":1: bad command' and 'errors in crontab file, can't install.' with exit status 1, and a subsequent 'crontab -l' reported 'no crontab for root' — the invalid table was refused, while writing the same text straight into /var/spool/cron/crontabs/root succeeded silently. o2, o3 and o4 whys are all true; crontab(5)/crontab(1) confirm that /etc/crontab and /etc/cron.d are a separate system-crontab mechanism and impose no line-count limit. Citation improved at concept level: crontab(5) documents the file format but not the -e workflow, so crontab(1) was added (and anacron(8) for the sibling item).

items.stem: A laptop was powered off overnight, missing its scheduled 03:00 cron job entirely; the job never ran once the machine came back on. Is plain cron broken?

options.text: No — cron simply skips a scheduled time that passes while the machine is off; `anacron` exists specifically to compensate for that
options.why: Cron has no memory of a missed schedule window; catching up on a run missed while powered off is a separate mechanism cron does not provide by itself.

options.text: Yes, cron should always run a missed job as soon as the machine powers back on
options.why: That catch-up behaviour is exactly what plain cron lacks and what `anacron` was built to add — expecting it from cron itself is the mistake here.

options.text: No, but the job must have been accidentally removed with `crontab -r` — cron drops a user's table automatically once one of its scheduled runs is missed
options.why: Nothing in the scenario suggests the crontab was removed; a missed run on a machine that was off is the far more direct and standard explanation.

options.text: Yes, and the fix is to switch the job to a `.timer` unit without `Persistent=true`
options.why: A timer without `Persistent=true` would show exactly the same behaviour as cron here; the catch-up property requires that setting specifically.

items.rationale: Cron simply skips a scheduled time that passes while the machine is powered off — it is not a fault. `anacron` exists to compensate for that on machines that are not on continuously, and a systemd timer with `Persistent=true` is the equivalent modern alternative. `crontab -l` would have confirmed the job was still scheduled all along.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed: anacron(8) states 'Unlike cron(8), it does not assume that the machine is running continuously. Hence, it can be used on machines that are not running 24 hours a day to control regular jobs as daily, weekly, and monthly jobs' — i.e. catch-up is anacron's job, not cron's, so a schedule that elapses while the machine is off is simply not run. o2's why is the direct contrapositive and is true. o4's why is confirmed by systemd.timer(5): Persistent= 'is useful to catch up on missed runs of the service when the timer was inactive', so a timer without it behaves like cron here. REFUTED AS AUTHORED on o3: the option text ended with its own why appended verbatim ('nothing in the scenario suggests the crontab was removed...'), so the option refuted itself. Rewritten with a false trailing claim (that cron drops a table after a missed run — no such behaviour exists in cron(8)/crontab(1)); why unchanged and still true. Re-checked: confirmed. Citation fixed at concept level: anacron(8) added, since crontab(5) never mentions anacron.

items.stem: A crontab line reads `30 4 1,15 * 5 /usr/local/bin/report.sh`. Both the day-of-month and day-of-week fields are restricted. When does the job actually run?

options.text: At 04:30 on the 1st and 15th of every month, and additionally at 04:30 every Friday
options.why: When both day fields are restricted, they combine with OR rather than AND, so either condition being satisfied triggers the run.

options.text: At 04:30, only on whichever day is both the 1st or 15th of the month and a Friday
options.why: The two day fields do not combine with AND; treating them that way would make the job run far less often than the five-field syntax specifies.

options.text: At 04:30 on the 1st and 15th of every month only; the day-of-week field is ignored when the day-of-month field is also set
options.why: Neither day field is ever silently ignored — when both are restricted, both take effect and combine with OR.

options.text: At 04:30 every Friday only; the day-of-month field is ignored when the day-of-week field is also set
options.why: Both restricted day fields take effect together via OR; the day-of-month field is not overridden by the day-of-week field.

items.rationale: When both the day-of-month and day-of-week fields are restricted (neither is `*`), cron combines them with OR rather than AND: the command runs when either matches. `30 4 1,15 * 5` therefore runs at 04:30 on the 1st and 15th and every Friday — a genuinely counter-intuitive rule worth memorising precisely. Entries like this are installed through `crontab -e`.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed verbatim against the cited source. crontab(5) says: 'The day of a command's execution can be specified in the following two fields - day of month, and day of week. If both fields are restricted (i.e., do not contain the "*" character), the command will be run when either field matches the current time. For example, "30 4 1,15 * 5" would cause a command to be run at 4:30 am on the 1st and 15th of each month, plus every Friday.' That is the item's exact expression, so the key is right and o2 (AND), o3 (day-of-week ignored) and o4 (day-of-month ignored) are all excluded by the same sentence; each why states the true rule. No defect found; no changes made.

items.stem: A crontab entry runs `backup.sh` (a bare command name, no path) and works perfectly when typed by hand at the shell, but silently does nothing on schedule. What is the standard diagnostic first step, and what is usually wrong?

options.text: Assume the environment: cron does not source shell startup files and supplies a minimal `PATH`, so a bare command name is often not found
options.why: Cron sets `SHELL` to `/bin/sh`, takes `HOME` and `LOGNAME` from the account's `/etc/passwd` row, and never sources `~/.bashrc` or `/etc/profile`, so a bare name resolved by an interactive shell's `PATH` may not resolve at all under cron.

options.text: The crontab syntax must contain a typo in one of the five time fields
options.why: A typo in the time fields would produce a run at the wrong time or not at all in a way distinguishable from this, but the described symptom — total silence with no output — is the signature of the sparse cron environment, not a scheduling error.

options.text: The job must have been removed by an accidental `crontab -r` — a crontab entry naming a command without an absolute path is rejected and discarded at install time
options.why: If the crontab had been removed, `crontab -l` would show it missing entirely; the scenario describes the entry running silently on schedule with no visible effect.

options.text: cron jobs cannot execute shell scripts at all, only single binaries
options.why: Cron happily executes shell scripts; the actual obstacle here is that the bare command name cannot be found under cron's minimal `PATH`.

items.rationale: The environment a cron job runs in is not the interactive shell's: cron sets a short default `PATH`, does not source `~/.bashrc` or `/etc/profile`, and takes `HOME`/`LOGNAME` from `/etc/passwd`. A bare command name that resolves fine interactively is the classic case that fails silently under cron; the fix is an absolute path or an explicit `PATH=` line in the crontab.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed on the cited source plus measurement. crontab(5) states 'SHELL is set to /bin/sh, and LOGNAME and HOME are set from the /etc/passwd line of the crontab's owner', which the key repeats exactly. crontab(5) does NOT mention PATH or shell startup files, so the rest of the key was verified empirically instead: 'docker run --rm debian:12' with cron installed and the entry '* * * * * env > /tmp/cronenv' produced exactly HOME=/root, LOGNAME=root, PATH=/usr/bin:/bin, SHELL=/bin/sh, PWD=/root, against an interactive PATH of /usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin in the same container — a strictly smaller PATH with no variables contributed by any startup file, which is precisely why a bare command name resolved interactively can fail under cron. o2's why is true, and o4's why is true (cron runs the command through /bin/sh, so scripts run normally). REFUTED AS AUTHORED on o3: the option text carried its own why appended verbatim. Rewritten with a false trailing claim (that crontab rejects entries lacking an absolute path — the measured run above installed and ran exactly such an entry); why unchanged. Re-checked: confirmed.

items.stem: An administrator enables `backup.service` directly, expecting it to run on a schedule the way a cron job would. What actually happens?

options.text: The service starts at every boot, which is not a schedule at all; the `.timer` unit is what needed to be enabled instead
options.why: A timer and its paired service are separate units, and enabling the service on its own only activates it at boot rather than on the timer's intended schedule.

options.text: The service runs on the schedule defined by `OnCalendar=` in the paired `.timer` unit, since they are linked automatically
options.why: Enabling the service does not consult the timer's schedule at all; only enabling the `.timer` unit itself causes activation on that schedule.

options.text: Nothing happens, since `.service` units cannot be enabled without a crontab entry pointing at them
options.why: A `.service` unit can be enabled on its own perfectly well; the issue is that doing so only activates it at boot, not on any recurring schedule.

options.text: The service is rejected by `systemctl` because it has no `OnCalendar=` directive of its own
options.why: `OnCalendar=` belongs to the `.timer` unit, not the `.service` unit; a service unit is not expected to carry that directive and enabling it does not fail for lacking one.

items.rationale: A timer unit is paired by name with a service unit it activates on a schedule. Enabling the service instead of the timer is the standard mistake: it makes the job run at every boot, which is not a schedule — the timer, not the service, is what must be enabled to get scheduled activation. `systemctl list-timers` shows every timer with its next and last activation.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed: systemd.timer(5) states 'For each timer file, a matching unit file must exist, describing the unit to activate when the timer elapses. By default, a service by the same name as the timer (except for the suffix) is activated' — the two are separate units, and the schedule (OnCalendar=) lives in the [Timer] section of the .timer unit only, so enabling the .service does not consult it. systemctl(1) confirms that 'enable' merely installs the unit's [Install] symlinks, which for a typical WantedBy=multi-user.target service means activation at boot rather than on any schedule. o2's why is therefore true, o3's why is true (a .service unit can be enabled on its own; no crontab entry is involved), and o4's why is true (OnCalendar= is a [Timer] directive; a service unit is not rejected for lacking one). No wrong key, no also-correct distractor, no self-refuting option. Citation strengthened at concept level with systemctl(1), which is where the enable-means-at-boot half of the key actually lives.

items.stem: Name two advantages a systemd timer has over plain cron for a scheduled job.

options.text: Output is captured in the queryable journal rather than mailed, and a missed run can be made up with `Persistent=true`
options.why: Both are direct consequences of a timer activating a fully-fledged systemd service rather than handing a command straight to a shell the way cron does.

options.text: Timers are simpler to write than crontab lines, and they require no separate unit file
options.why: A timer requires a separate `.timer` unit paired with a `.service` unit — genuinely more moving parts than a single crontab line, not fewer.

options.text: Timers run with a full interactive shell environment, unlike cron — the service a timer activates is started from a login shell that sources the user's profile
options.why: The examinable advantages are journal logging, dependency handling and catch-up behaviour — a full interactive environment is not one of them.

options.text: Timers can run system-wide scripts, while cron is restricted to per-user jobs only — every crontab lives in a per-user spool file and cron has no system-wide table
options.why: System-wide scheduled jobs exist under plain cron too, via `/etc/crontab` and `/etc/cron.d/`; that is not a capability unique to timers.

items.rationale: Because a timer activates a real systemd service rather than handing a command to a shell, it inherits the manager's features automatically: output captured in the journal (queryable with `journalctl -u`), full dependency ordering, and — with `Persistent=true` — the ability to catch up on a run missed while the machine was off.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed: systemd.timer(5) documents Persistent= as storing the last trigger time on disk so that 'the service unit is triggered immediately if it would have been triggered at least once during the time when the timer was inactive... useful to catch up on missed runs', and systemd-journald.service(8) documents that the journal collects the standard output and standard error of started units and is queried with journalctl. o2's why is true (a timer needs a paired .service unit, so it is more moving parts, not fewer). REFUTED AS AUTHORED on both o3 and o4: each option text ended with its own why appended verbatim, so both announced their own wrongness. Both were rewritten with false trailing claims — a timer's service is not started from a login shell and does not source a profile (systemd.exec(5) environment, not a shell), and crontab(5) documents /etc/crontab and /etc/cron.d as system-wide cron tables, contradicting o4's new tail. Whys unchanged and both remain true. Re-checked: confirmed.

items.stem: An administrator is following a live tail of a busy log with `tail -f` when the log gets rotated by `logrotate` and renamed aside. New entries stop appearing. Which command survives rotation, and why?

options.text: `tail -F`, because it follows the file by name and reopens it after a rename, rather than staying attached to the old inode
options.why: `-f` keeps holding the original file descriptor, which now points at the renamed, no-longer-growing file; `-F` notices the name has a fresh file and reopens it.

options.text: `tail -f` should already handle rotation correctly, since it is designed to follow a growing log
options.why: `-f` stays with the original inode it opened, which is exactly what stops updating the moment the log is rotated away under a new name.

options.text: `less +F`, since only `less` supports following a log across rotation — its F command reopens the file by name as soon as the inode behind it changes
options.why: less(1) says the F command behaves similarly to `tail -f`, and that without `--follow-name` less keeps displaying the original file when it is renamed; the option that specifically reopens by name is `tail -F`.

options.text: Neither survives rotation; the session must be restarted manually every time a log rotates
options.why: `tail -F` is specifically designed to survive rotation by reopening the file under its name, so a manual restart is not required.

items.rationale: `tail -f` follows the specific file descriptor it opened, which after rotation still points at the old, now-static file under its renamed path. `tail -F` follows the *name* instead, reopening the newly created file once rotation replaces it — the option that keeps working across a rotation.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against tail(1): '-f, --follow[={name|descriptor}] ... an absent option argument means descriptor', '-F same as --follow=name --retry', and '--max-unchanged-stats=N: with --follow=name, reopen a FILE which has not changed size after N iterations to see if it has been unlinked or renamed (this is the usual case of rotated log files)'. That settles both the key and o2's why. o4's why is true by the same text. REFUTED AS AUTHORED on o3, twice over: the option text carried its own why appended verbatim, and the why's claim about less was unsourced. Rewritten — the text now ends in a false claim (that less's F reopens by name), and the why now quotes less(1), which states that the F command behaves 'similar to the tail -f command' and that only '--follow-name' makes less 'periodically attempt to reopen the file by name'. Re-checked: confirmed. Citation refuted as authored and fixed at concept level: the concept cited only FHS 3.0, which locates /var/log but says nothing about tail; tail(1) and less(1) were added.

items.stem: A filter is set to capture severity level 3 (Error) and above. Does it also capture Warning-level messages?

options.text: No — severity 3 and above means levels 3, 2, 1 and 0, and Warning is level 4, a less severe level than 3
options.why: The scale runs opposite to intuition: the most severe level has the lowest number, so "level 3 and above" means numerically lower, more severe levels only.

options.text: Yes, "level 3 and above" naturally includes Warning since it feels like a lesser problem than Error
options.why: Numerically, Warning (4) is a higher number than Error (3), and on this inverted scale a higher number is less severe, so it falls outside the filter.

options.text: It depends on the facility the message was logged under, not the severity level — a severity filter matches only messages carrying the daemon facility
options.why: Facility identifies the source subsystem and is a separate dimension from severity; it does not change whether a given severity number is captured by this filter.

options.text: Yes, because syslog severities count upward from least to most severe starting at 1
options.why: The scale starts at 0 for Emergency, the most severe level, and counts upward toward less severe levels, the opposite of what this option describes.

items.rationale: Syslog severity runs from Emergency (0) as most severe down to Debug (7) as least severe — the numbering is inverted from intuition. Filtering to "level 3 and above" in severity means 3, 2, 1 and 0 (Error through Emergency), which does not include Warning at level 4.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against RFC 5424 Table 2, read directly: 0 Emergency, 1 Alert, 2 Critical, 3 Error, 4 Warning, 5 Notice, 6 Informational, 7 Debug, with 'Severity values MUST be in the range of 0 to 7 inclusive'. Warning is 4, numerically above Error at 3, so a filter at 'Error and above' in severity captures 3, 2, 1, 0 only — which journalctl(1) states operationally for -p: 'If a single log level is specified, all messages with this log level or a lower (hence more important) log level are shown.' o2's and o4's whys are both true against the same table (the scale starts at 0 = Emergency and counts upward toward less severe). REFUTED AS AUTHORED on o3: the option text ended with its own why appended verbatim. Rewritten with a false trailing claim (that a severity filter matches only the daemon facility); the why is unchanged and remains true — RFC 5424 Table 1 shows facility as an independent 0-23 dimension. Re-checked: confirmed. journalctl(1) added at concept level because the item turns on filter semantics, which RFC 5424 does not define.

items.stem: A badly behaved application logs routine, harmless status messages at Error severity. What is the consequence for a monitoring filter tuned to alert on Error and above?

options.text: It floods the filter with false alarms, because severity is a claim by the emitting program, not an assessment by the logging system
options.why: The logging system has no way to second-guess the severity a program chooses to attach to its own messages, so a badly calibrated emitter degrades any filter built on that scale.

options.text: Nothing changes, since the logging system automatically re-classifies mislabelled messages — the severity is recomputed from the message text as it is written to the log
options.why: No such automatic re-classification happens; the logging system records whatever severity the emitting program attaches to a message.

options.text: The messages are silently dropped, since Error severity from a non-critical process is filtered out by default
options.why: There is no default behaviour that drops messages based on which process emitted them; the messages pass through at the severity the application chose.

options.text: The facility field automatically corrects the severity based on which subsystem is logging
options.why: Facility identifies the source subsystem and is independent of severity; it does not adjust or override the severity a message carries.

items.rationale: Severity is set by whichever program emits the message, not assessed independently by the logging system. A badly behaved application logging routine chatter at Error level floods any filter tuned to catch real problems at that severity, since the system has no mechanism to override the emitter's own claim.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed: RFC 5424 defines the PRI value as computed by the originator from its own Facility and Severity ('The Priority value is calculated by first multiplying the Facility number by 8 and then adding the numerical value of the Severity'), and describes Facility and Severity values as 'not normative but often used ... for purely informational purposes' — the protocol provides no mechanism by which a collector re-derives severity, so the emitter's claim is what a filter sees. journalctl(1)'s -p filters on exactly that recorded priority. o3's why is true (nothing drops messages by emitting process by default) and o4's why is true (facility is independent of severity). REFUTED AS AUTHORED on o2: the option text ended with its own why appended verbatim. Rewritten with a false trailing claim (that severity is recomputed from message text), which RFC 5424 contradicts; why unchanged. Re-checked: confirmed.

items.stem: After a crash, `journalctl -b -1` returns nothing at all, as if the previous boot never happened. What is the most likely explanation, and what confirms it?

options.text: The journal is volatile: without `/var/log/journal` existing, it lives under `/run` and is discarded at every reboot; `journalctl --list-boots` confirms what is retained
options.why: By default the journal is persistent only if `/var/log/journal` exists; otherwise it is memory-backed and vanishes at the very reboot that would otherwise let it be inspected.

options.text: `journalctl` itself must be malfunctioning, since a crash should always leave some trace
options.why: The tool is working correctly; an empty result for the previous boot is the expected behaviour of a volatile, non-persistent journal, not a fault in `journalctl`.

options.text: The messages must be in `/var/log/syslog` instead, since journald never captures kernel or crash messages
options.why: journald does capture kernel and crash-time messages when persistent storage exists; the issue here is that persistence was never configured at all.

options.text: `-b -1` is the wrong syntax and should instead be `-b 1` to see the previous boot — journalctl numbers boots forward from the first one ever recorded and rejects negative offsets outright
options.why: `-b -1` is the correct syntax for the boot before the current one; the empty result is a persistence problem, not a syntax error.

items.rationale: The journal is persistent only if `/var/log/journal` exists; otherwise it lives in `/run/log/journal`, which is memory-backed and discarded at every reboot. `journalctl --list-boots` shows what is actually retained, and if nothing is, that absence is itself the finding — enabling persistent storage is the first remediation.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed verbatim against the cited source. systemd-journald.service(8): 'The journal service stores log data either persistently below /var/log/journal or in a volatile way below /run/log/journal/ (in the latter case, it is lost at reboot). By default, log data is stored persistently if /var/log/journal/ exists during boot, with an implicit fallback to volatile storage otherwise.' journalctl(1) confirms --list-boots shows 'a tabular list of boot numbers (relative to the current boot), their IDs, and the timestamps of the first and last message pertaining to the boot', which is what makes the absence visible. o2's and o3's whys are true. REFUTED AS AUTHORED on o4: the option text ended with its own why appended verbatim. Rewritten with a false trailing claim; journalctl(1) states of the -b offset that 'Negative values mean earlier boots and positive values mean later boots', so the new tail is false and the why remains true. Re-checked: confirmed. journalctl(1) added at concept level, since journald(8) does not document journalctl's options. Distractor `o4` was then lengthened, without changing its meaning or its why, to remove the key-is-longest length cue that stripping the self-refuting padding had exposed.

items.stem: A service will not start. What is the diagnostic order across `systemctl status`, `journalctl -u <unit> -b`, and `journalctl -p err -b`?

options.text: `systemctl status <unit>` for the last few lines and exit status, then `journalctl -u <unit> -b` for everything that unit logged this boot, then `journalctl -p err -b` to widen the search to any failing dependency
options.why: Working from the narrowest, fastest signal outward finds the direct cause quickly and, if that is inconclusive, widens to catch a dependency that failed first and took the service down with it.

options.text: `journalctl -p err -b` first, since severity filtering always finds the root cause fastest regardless of scope, and narrows to the failing unit by itself
options.why: Starting with a system-wide severity filter skips the fastest, most direct signal — the unit's own status and its own log entries — which usually explains the failure on its own.

options.text: `journalctl -u <unit> -f` first, to watch it fail live before checking anything else — `-f` replays everything the unit logged during this boot and only then begins following new entries as they arrive
options.why: Following live only helps while reproducing the failure in real time; the described scenario is investigating a failure that has already occurred, for which status and boot logs come first.

options.text: `journalctl -p err -b` alone is sufficient, and the other two commands add nothing a severity-wide sweep of the current boot has not already surfaced
options.why: A severity-wide filter can miss a failure logged at a lower severity or buried among many other units' errors; the unit-specific commands narrow the search far more directly.

items.rationale: `systemctl status <unit>` gives the fastest read — the last few lines and exit status. `journalctl -u` narrowed to the unit and `journalctl -b` narrowed to this boot together widen to everything that unit logged this boot. `journalctl -p err` widens further still, to catch a dependency that failed first and is the real cause; `journalctl -f` is the live-following variant used while reproducing a fault in real time.

verification.reasoning: Each command's semantics is documented and was checked: journalctl(1) defines -u as 'Show messages for the specified systemd unit', -b as limiting output to a given boot, -p as showing 'all messages with this log level or a lower (hence more important) log level', and -f as showing 'only the most recent journal entries, and continuously print new entries as they are appended'. The KEY'S ORDERING, however, is a best-practice judgement rather than a documented rule: no cited source states that status should precede unit logs which should precede a severity-wide sweep. Recorded honestly as such — the key is defensible because it moves from narrowest to widest scope and each step is a real capability of the named command, and no distractor is also correct: o2 and o4 both propose a system-wide severity filter in place of unit-scoped evidence, and their whys are true. REFUTED AS AUTHORED on o3: the option text ended with its own why appended verbatim. Rewritten with a false trailing claim, since journalctl(1) says -f shows 'only the most recent journal entries' rather than replaying the boot; why unchanged. Re-checked: confirmed. Distractor `o3` was then lengthened, without changing its meaning or its why, to remove the key-is-longest length cue that stripping the self-refuting padding had exposed.

items.stem: A huge log file is deleted by hand to free disk space, but `df -h` still reports the filesystem as full afterward. Why, and what is the correct long-term fix?

options.text: The daemon still has the file open, so its blocks stay allocated until the descriptor closes; the fix is scheduled log rotation, not manual deletion
options.why: Deleting a file a process still holds open frees no space until that process closes or restarts, and rotation is what avoids ever needing manual deletion again.

options.text: `df -h` is simply slow to update and will reflect the freed space after a short wait
options.why: The reported figure will not change on its own; the blocks remain allocated as long as the daemon keeps the deleted file's descriptor open, however long that is.

options.text: The log must actually be compressed already, which is why deleting it did not free space
options.why: Compression status has nothing to do with whether deleting the file frees its blocks; the cause here is an open file descriptor held by a running process.

options.text: The filesystem must have run out of inodes rather than blocks — removing one very large file frees the blocks it occupied but never releases the inode that indexed them
options.why: Inode exhaustion produces a distinct "No space left" symptom with free blocks still showing; this scenario describes blocks that remain allocated, consistent with a held-open deleted file.

items.rationale: Removing a file a daemon still has open frees no space at all until that descriptor closes, which is exactly the `df`/`du` discrepancy this concept explains. The durable fix is configuring log rotation so files never grow unbounded in the first place, rather than deleting a huge log after the fact.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed against unlink(2), read directly: 'If the name was the last link to a file and no processes have the file open, the file is deleted and the space it was using is made available for reuse. If the name was the last link to a file but any processes still have the file open, the file will remain in existence until the last file descriptor referring to it is closed.' That is exactly the key's mechanism. o2's why and o3's why are both true. REFUTED AS AUTHORED on o4: the option text ended with its own why appended verbatim. Rewritten with a false trailing claim — unlink(2) shows the inode is released once the last link and last descriptor are gone — while the why is unchanged and still true. Re-checked: confirmed. Citation refuted as authored: neither logrotate(8) nor journald(8) documents the held-open-descriptor behaviour the item turns on; unlink(2) was added at concept level. This is the same defect class recorded earlier in this cycle for df(1). Distractor `o4` was then lengthened, without changing its meaning or its why, to remove the key-is-longest length cue that stripping the self-refuting padding had exposed.

items.stem: A daemon cannot be signalled to reopen its log file after rotation, but the log still must not grow unbounded. Which `logrotate` directive fits, and what is its cost?

options.text: `copytruncate`, which copies the log aside and truncates the original in place — at the cost of losing whatever is written between the copy and the truncate
options.why: Copying then truncating keeps the daemon writing to the same inode without needing to signal it, but there is a small window where in-flight writes can be lost.

options.text: `postrotate`, since it is the directive used whenever a daemon cannot be signalled — the script it runs swaps the daemon's open file descriptor from outside the process
options.why: A `postrotate` script is exactly the mechanism used to signal a daemon; it is the wrong choice for a daemon that specifically cannot be signalled.

options.text: `compress`, since compressing the rotated file avoids needing to signal the daemon at all
options.why: Compression controls whether old generations are stored compressed; it has no bearing on whether the daemon needs to be told to reopen its log file.

options.text: `delaycompress`, which defers the problem to the next rotation cycle instead of solving it
options.why: logrotate(8) presents `delaycompress` as a way to avoid compressing a file a program may still be writing to; it changes only when compression happens, and leaves the daemon writing to the renamed file, so the new log stays empty and the old one keeps growing.

items.rationale: `copytruncate` copies the log's contents aside and truncates the original file in place, so a daemon that cannot be signalled keeps writing to the same inode without interruption — at the cost of losing anything written in the brief window between the copy and the truncate.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed verbatim against logrotate(8): 'copytruncate: Truncate the original log file to zero size in place after creating a copy... It can be used when some program cannot be told to close its logfile and thus might continue writing (appending) to the previous log file forever. Note that there is a very small time slice between copying the file and truncating it, so some logging data might be lost.' Both halves of the key — the mechanism and its cost — are that sentence pair. o3's why is true. REFUTED AS AUTHORED on o2: the option text ended with its own why appended verbatim; rewritten with a false trailing claim (no external script can swap a running process's descriptor), why unchanged. ALSO REFUTED AS AUTHORED on o4's why, which claimed delaycompress 'does not address the stated problem at all' — logrotate(8) actually introduces delaycompress for the very case where 'some program cannot be told to close its logfile and thus might continue writing to the previous log file for some time', so the original why overstated and was partly false. Rewritten to say what is true: delaycompress changes only when compression happens and still leaves the daemon writing to the renamed file. Re-checked both: confirmed.

items.stem: Put the five stages of the boot process in order, from power-on to a running system.

options.text: Firmware, bootloader, kernel plus initramfs, PID 1 (the init system), then units until the default target
options.why: Each stage hands control to the next: firmware finds a boot device, the bootloader loads the kernel, the kernel mounts the real root, and the init system brings up the rest.

options.text: Bootloader, firmware, kernel, units, then PID 1 — on modern machines the bootloader is what loads the firmware into memory
options.why: Firmware runs first, before any bootloader can be found or executed — this ordering has the first two stages reversed.

options.text: Firmware, kernel, bootloader, PID 1, then units — the kernel starts first and then invokes a bootloader to locate the root filesystem
options.why: The bootloader runs before the kernel, not after it — the kernel cannot be loaded until the bootloader has found and loaded it into memory.

options.text: Firmware, bootloader, PID 1, kernel, then units
options.why: PID 1 cannot start before the kernel does, since the kernel is what starts PID 1 in the first place — the third and fourth stages are swapped here.

items.rationale: The ordered handover is: firmware initialises hardware and finds a boot device; the bootloader loads the kernel and an initramfs; the kernel initialises and mounts the real root filesystem; it starts PID 1; and the init system activates units until the default target is reached.

verification.reasoning: Key confirmed verbatim against bootup(7): 'Immediately after power-up, the system firmware will do minimal hardware initialization, and hand control over to a boot loader (e.g. systemd-boot(7) or GRUB) stored on a persistent storage device. This boot loader will then invoke an OS kernel from disk... The kernel (optionally) mounts an in-memory file system, which looks for the root file system. Nowadays this is implemented as an initramfs', after which systemd(1) manages units. That is the item's five-stage order exactly. o4's why is true (the kernel starts PID 1). REFUTED AS AUTHORED on o2 and o3: both option texts ended with their own why appended verbatim. Both were rewritten with false trailing claims that bootup(7) contradicts directly (firmware runs before any boot loader; the boot loader invokes the kernel, not the reverse); both whys are unchanged and remain true. Re-checked: confirmed. Citation refuted as authored: systemd(1) and systemd.special(7) cover PID 1 and targets but not the firmware/bootloader/kernel handover; bootup(7) was added at concept level.

items.stem: `systemd-analyze blame` names a unit that took 30 seconds during a slow boot, but nothing else was waiting on that unit while it ran. Was it the cause of the slow boot?

options.text: Not necessarily — `blame` measures duration, not delay, and a unit that runs in parallel with nothing waiting on it costs nothing to boot time
options.why: Because activation happens in parallel wherever dependencies allow, a slow unit only actually delays boot if something else is blocked waiting for it to finish.

options.text: Yes, the slowest-duration unit in `blame`'s output is always what held boot up
options.why: Duration alone does not establish delay when units run in parallel; `systemd-analyze critical-chain` is what shows the ordering chain that actually determined boot time.

options.text: No, because `blame` only reports on the firmware phase, which happens before Linux is even running
options.why: `blame` reports how long userspace units spent initialising; the firmware runs earlier still, before anything on disk has been read, and is outside what the command measures.

options.text: No, but only because the unit must have failed rather than merely run slowly — `blame` lists only units that exited non-zero, so appearing in its output is itself the failure signal
options.why: Nothing in the scenario suggests the unit failed; it ran successfully but slowly, and the question is whether that slowness delayed anything else.

items.rationale: systemd activates units in parallel wherever the dependency graph allows, so `blame`'s ranking by duration does not by itself show what delayed boot. `systemd-analyze critical-chain` identifies the actual ordering chain that determined when boot converged, which a merely slow but unwaited-on unit does not appear on.

So blame ranks duration, not delay, exactly as the key says, and o2's why is true. o3's why is true — blame reports units' 'activating' time, not the firmware phase.
